title: Ezekiel Lewis Talks New Epic Records CEO Gig & the Art of A&R: ‘It’s Not About Genres. It’s About Artists’
summary: In the latest episode of Billboard On the Record, Lewis sits down to talk about his new role as Epic's CEO/chairman for the first time.
contentText:
Ezekiel “Zeke” Lewis doesn’t have the typical origin story of a major label CEO. He got his start as a Grammy-winning songwriter and producer in Atlanta, co-penning songs like “One Less Lonely Girl” by Justin Bieber and “The Way I Are” by Timbaland , often with his collective The Clutch, before he made his jump to the boardroom. Today, however, Lewis sees the creative journey as critical to his understanding of the music business and what artists need from their industry partners.

“When I got inside the building, I realized that my songwriting career and the fact that I had achieved some success was a miracle,” he explains. He was fascinated by “the way music moves through buildings,” and he found a new calling to “get inside to help creators” navigate the industry with greater success.

Molly Neuman on the Evolution of Independent Music From the ’90s to Now: ‘It Was a High-Risk Business’

First, he built up his own publishing house, Bar Music Group. Then he landed an A&R gig at Motown Records, where he worked his way up the ladder to become senior vp of A&R by the time he left in 2018. That job was also where he first worked with legendary label executive Sylvia Rhone , who he says taught him to “be diligent, never give up and never take no for an answer,” as he puts it. But when Rhone left the job and took a role at Sony Music’s Epic Records, where she eventually rose to become its CEO/chairman, she courted Lewis to follow her and scout the next generation of talent there.

As Lewis has advanced in his career at Epic, he’s played a pivotal role in shaping the careers of 21 Savage, Madison Beer, BIA, Black Eyed Peas, DDG, Future, GIVĒON, Zara Larsson, Mariah the Scientist, Travis Scott, Southside, Meghan Trainor and Tyla. When Rhone stepped away in 2025, rumors swirled that Lewis was being eyed as her successor. In March, the confirmation finally came that Lewis had been appointed CEO/chairman of Epic.

Lewis joins the latest episode of Billboard On the Record in his first-ever interview as CEO and chairman to discuss what it takes to run a successful label in 2026, how he approaches A&R, and how his songwriting career shaped his leadership in the boardroom.

You have built up your whole business career in music in A&R. This historically has been a role held often by creative people. I think of George Martin, producer and A&R for The Beatles, as a prime example. Now, however, A&R is more data-driven and typically not held by creatives. Why have we moved away from A&R having creative experience?

I don’t accept that. I hear people say a lot of the job of A&R has changed, and I’m thinking to myself, “Actually no, it hasn’t.” I think the job of A&R has and always will be to creatively direct and help to collaborate with the artist, in terms of the direction of the music and the touch and the taste and the feel of a project. I don’t think that’s changed. I think obviously people put research into the A&R bucket, but research is its own thing. A&R is a different thing.

Questlove on the History of Sampling, From Public Enemy to Today: ‘I See AI as a Parallel to Sampling Culture’

Now that you’re helming Epic, how do you structure the A&R department, given that is your philosophy?

There is a research aspect of A&R, and then there is what I call record-making A&Rs. There’s two different aspects, and we plug in with the artists where needed. And every artist needs a different thing, you know? People like Future, who are well established, might just want your opinion on a thing, and maybe you help him curate the tracklist, or maybe you give him an opinion if he asks you for it. Travis Scott — another example where he’s a force of his own — but, for example, for the Jack Boys project, he actually had me help get Tyla one of those records. So it’s a light touch. It just depends on what the artists need, and some artists need a lot more.

How do you navigate that? You don’t want to offend an artist by stepping in and commandeering their project .

You have to be invited, and upon invitation you need to add value.

What is a project that you really feel like you worked on side-by-side with the artist, helping them mold their music?

That would certainly be Tyla. Obviously, [it started with] signing her from Johannesburg and then cultivating every aspect of the process of making her first record and even her second record.

In the case of Tyla, you signed her over Zoom during the pandemic. When you were courting her to sign to Epic, could you still tell that she had the X factor through the screen?

Absolutely. And this is the thing that’s hardest to articulate in the A&R process, which is the beginning of the process. That’s the intangible nature of that X factor that you’re describing in words, but absolutely, you could see it immediately that she was going to be someone.

It can’t be underestimated how much TikTok and short-form video changed the game for promoting records. Before TikTok, there were still gatekeepers who a label could call that would significantly help break a song — Spotify playlisters, disc jockeys, press. Then TikTok comes around and it’s all discovery driven by algorithms. As much as labels can study the algorithm, it’s ultimately unknowable. How do you think that shift impacted what a record label can provide for an artist?

I always say our job, both in A&R and as a team in general, is to create opportunities where magic can happen. And so you want to put the artist in a space where the best parts of them can be highlighted. Then, at that point, if the right people see that, then you can trigger the algorithm…because you created the environment where that magic could happen.

In the case of Tyla, it was when she did the show in Rwanda. We were supporting her with tour support and other things at the time, and so she’s able to be there and come up with this brilliant idea to pour the water on her back as she’s performing the song “Water” as part of the choreography, and that just caught fire and made people pay attention to the song, which ultimately became a big hit.

A conversation that started to take place during the pandemic is, you can’t skip steps, and yet a lot of artists were at that time. They’d have a viral hit out of nowhere, immediately start a label bidding war and meanwhile these artists have never played a show —

I regret that that happened. I mean, look, people were able to benefit from having these moments of virality or whatnot, but I do think it affected the long tail and the elongation of the careers of so many would-be great artists because those deals were inflated, and so the companies were behind eight ball financially because they wanted to work with those artists and they wanted to make them great.

You know, when you are behind the eight ball on a deal for a developing artist, and then you don’t have success immediately following, it could put you in a position where [a label] won’t be able to invest in the artist where [they normally] would. If you were able to do [a deal that was] reasonable — and I tell some of my attorney friends all the time — I don’t know if we’re serving the artist correctly when we’re front-loading the deals.

Like super high advances?
